title: [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois..., pages 650 bis à 787, dont table des matières] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the continuation of the Longue Marche manuscript (pages 650 bis–787). The 'L-structures' are very likely the discrete 'groupe à lacets' structures on surface groups: the conjugacy classes of loops around the punctures, plus orientation data. On the previous page Grothendieck defines, for a discrete group pi, L(pi) as the direct limit over finite-index normal subgroups pi_i of the sets L_0^G(pi_i) of pi-invariant lacet-structures on pi_i. In other words, an L-structure on pi is a lacet structure on some finite-index subgroup, taken up to commensurability. A pair (pi, lambda) is an 'L-groupe', and pi_i is a 'subgroup of definition'.

On this page he finishes the statement that, for pi' of finite index in pi, the induction map L(pi) -> L(pi') is injective. Its image is the set of L-structures on pi' that are 'invariant under pi' in the evident sense.

Special case: an extension 1 -> pi_0 -> pi -> G -> 1 with G finite. The L-structures on pi correspond to the L-structures on pi_0 that are invariant under the outer action pi/pi_0 = G -> Autext(pi_0).

NB: pi |-> L(pi) is a functor on 'outer groups', with outer isomorphisms as arrows.

Standard example: X a 0-connected 'multiplicity' (orbifold/stack, here a surface) of finite type and G a finite group acting on X. Then pi = pi_1(X,G;a) is the equivariant fundamental group, i.e. pi_1 of the quotient stack [X/G]. It sits in 1 -> pi_1(X,a) -> pi -> G -> 1. The canonical lacet structure on pi_1(X,a) is G-invariant, so it gives an L-structure on pi.

The next page states the converse: every L-group arises this way. Grothendieck calls this deep and essentially equivalent to the existence of fixed points of finite subgroups of Teichmüller modular groups. This is the Nielsen realization problem, solved by Kerckhoff in 1983. He also asks for a 2-categorical equivalence between L-groups and orbifold surfaces of finite type with weighted divisors (orbifold points with multiplicities in N*).
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. The claimed bijection for finite-index subgroups is correct, given that lacet structures are compatible with restriction to finite-index subgroups.
One implicit assumption: for 'invariance by pi/pi_0 -> Autext(pi_0)' to make sense, L(pi_0) must be functorial for outer automorphisms. Grothendieck notes this in the NB.

ideas.what: Commensurability-invariant 'L-structure' on a discrete group, defined as a direct limit over finite-index normal subgroups of invariant lacet structures
ideas.modern_name: virtual peripheral (cusp) structure on virtually surface groups; orbifold fundamental group structure
ideas.where_published: Related 'groupes à lacets' appear in La Longue Marche (1981, circulated)

ideas.what: Descent of L-structures along finite extensions: L(pi) equals the G-invariants of L(pi_0) under the outer action
ideas.modern_name: Galois descent of structure along a finite extension of groups

ideas.what: Equivariant fundamental group pi_1(X,G;a) of a finite group acting on a multiplicity, with exact sequence 1 -> pi_1(X) -> pi -> G -> 1
ideas.modern_name: fundamental group of quotient stack / orbifold [X/G]
ideas.where_published: SGA1 exposé V-style equivariant constructions; La Longue Marche

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine set-up of L-structures and their descent through finite extensions, plus the standard orbifold example. The interesting remark (link to Nielsen realization via fixed points of finite subgroups of Teichmüller groups) is on the next page and was proved by Kerckhoff in 1983. Its group-theoretic form is also known (Zieschang, Eckmann–Müller).
